sentence: Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic that the NHS describes as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections, such as cystitis.
It is available only with a prescription.
It can also be prescribed to help prevent urinary tract infections from coming back.
MedlinePlus places it in a class of medicines called antibiotics, which work by killing the bacteria that cause infection.
Like other antibiotics, it does not work for colds, flu or other viral infections.
NICE guidance on lower urinary tract infections sets out where nitrofurantoin can be used, and says it is not recommended for men with suspected prostate involvement.
note: NICE NG109 recommendations via search summary.

sentence: West Yorkshire NHS prescribing guidance adds that it is unsuitable for upper urinary tract infections, such as kidney infections.
note: Search summary of the West Yorkshire guidance; blended with NHS pages.

sentence: The NHS says nitrofurantoin is best taken with or after a meal or snack, which helps the body absorb it and helps prevent an upset stomach.
note: Search summary of about and how-and-when pages.

sentence: Tablets and capsules are swallowed whole rather than chewed or broken.
For liquid forms, the NHS notes that a household teaspoon does not measure the right amount.
The NHS page also explains what to do about a missed dose, and says a double dose is not taken to make up for a forgotten one.
The NHS stresses the importance of continuing until the course is finished, even after feeling better, to stop the infection coming back.
MedlinePlus likewise says that stopping early or skipping doses can make an infection harder to treat and may promote resistance.
The NHS lists nausea, diarrhoea, loss of appetite and headaches as the usual side effects.
Dark yellow or brown urine also occurs, and the NHS describes it as harmless.
The urine returns to its usual colour once the medicine is stopped.
Side effects usually go away when the medicine is stopped, and taking it with or after food can ease nausea.
The NHS says serious side effects are rare.
They include lung problems, liver problems such as jaundice and hepatitis, and allergic reactions.
Anaphylaxis, a severe allergic reaction, means calling 999 for an ambulance, while the NHS route for other serious side effects is NHS 111.
A local NHS leaflet describes shortness of breath or a lingering cough as lung symptoms needing urgent medical advice, and yellowing of the skin or eyes as a possible sign of liver effects.
note: Kent and Medway formulary patient leaflet (search summary).

sentence: The NHS says nitrofurantoin will not usually affect the ability to drive, ride a bike or use machinery.
The NHS says most adults and children can take nitrofurantoin, but it is not suitable for everyone.
Previous allergic reactions or serious side effects from it, a lung condition, severe kidney problems, diabetes, anaemia, vitamin B deficiency and porphyria are all listed as reasons to check first.
The NHS also lists G6PD deficiency, liver problems and conditions causing severe weakness.
note: Summary says a companion NHS page lists these; pages blended.

sentence: The NHS says nitrofurantoin can usually be taken earlier in pregnancy.
A doctor may not recommend it later on, because it can affect the baby's red blood cells.
The NHS also notes that treating a urinary tract infection during pregnancy is important.
Small amounts pass into breast milk and are unlikely to cause side effects in a baby, though the NHS advises checking with a doctor or pharmacist first.
NHS specialist advice is to avoid it if the infant has G6PD deficiency or jaundice, because of the risk of haemolytic anaemia.
Among other medicines, MedlinePlus lists antacids as a nonprescription product that may interact.
NHS pharmacy guidance says magnesium trisilicate may reduce absorption.
It adds that products which make urine less acidic, such as some cystitis remedies containing potassium citrate or sodium bicarbonate, weaken the antibiotic's action.
MedlinePlus also notes that nitrofurantoin can cause false results on urine tests for glucose.
Dark yellow or brown urine is a known effect of nitrofurantoin, and the NHS describes it as harmless.
The urine goes back to its usual colour once the medicine has been stopped.
West Yorkshire NHS prescribing guidance says nitrofurantoin is unsuitable for upper urinary tract infections, which include kidney infections.
The NHS describes it as a medicine for lower urinary tract infections such as cystitis.
No: MedlinePlus says antibiotics such as nitrofurantoin will not work for colds, flu or other viral infections.
